Waste Allocation as a Network

  • A network model’s decisions are flows; its constraints are conservation at each node.
  • An optional facility gets a binary: fixed cost \(\times\, Y_j\), and flow in \(\leq K_j Y_j\).

Decisions Under Uncertainty

Decisions Made in Advance

  • Reservoir: summer release targets are set in spring, before the summer’s inflow is known.
  • Grid: plants are committed the day before, before tomorrow’s wind is known (Oct 28).

In both, the decision comes first and adjusting afterwards costs money.

About five minutes. The reservoir schematic is the one from the first week of the course. The manager has to commit to a release plan before knowing the inflow; once the inflow arrives, there is some room to adjust (cut releases, buy water elsewhere, spill), but adjustments cost something. The grid operator is the same: plants are committed a day ahead, and if the wind is lower than expected, expensive peaking plants make up the difference. Today is about choosing the first decision knowing that the later adjustments will happen. Wednesday’s lecture and Monday’s lab use the reservoir.

Certainty and Linear Programming

Certainty was the third assumption of linear programming (with linearity and divisibility): every number in the model is known.

Common practice: solve with best estimates, then stress-test the plan (Monte Carlo, safety margins).

Alternative: put the uncertainty in the model, as a set of scenarios with probabilities, and optimize the expected outcome.

About three minutes. We relaxed divisibility with mixed integer programming; today we relax certainty. The common approach treats uncertainty after the fact: optimize for the average, then check how the plan does. The alternative builds the scenarios into the optimization itself, so the plan already accounts for having to adjust later.

Act, Learn, Act

  1. Make a decision \(x\) under uncertainty (here and now).
  2. Observe which scenario happens.
  3. Make a recourse decision that compensates for \(x\) in that scenario.

Dispatch version: dispatch hour 1, get better forecasts of demand and wind, re-dispatch (possibly with expensive peakers) to meet hour 2.

About three minutes. This is the two-stage structure. The first-stage decision is made once. The recourse decision is made after learning which scenario occurred, so there is one recourse decision per scenario. The goal is a first decision that leaves good options for every scenario, weighted by how likely each is.

The Farmer’s Problem

The Farmer’s Problem

A farmer has 500 acres for wheat, corn, and sugar beets. How much of each should they plant? (Birge & Louveaux, 2011)

  • Planting: $150, $230, $260 per acre.
  • Feed: 200 T wheat, 240 T corn; extra sells for $170, $150/T; buying costs 40% more.
  • Beets: $36/T up to 6,000 T, then $10/T.
  • Yields: 2.5, 3, 20 T/acre on average; ±20% in good and bad years, each with probability 1/3.

About two minutes. This is a classic example from Birge and Louveaux’s textbook on stochastic programming. Planting happens before the yield is known; buying and selling happen after the harvest. The beet quota matters: beets are very profitable up to 6,000 tonnes and barely worth growing beyond.

Formulation for One Known Year

\(x_i\): acres planted; \(y_i\): T bought; \(z_i\): T sold (\(z_3\) beets at the quota price, \(z_4\) above it).

\[ \begin{aligned} \max_{x, y, z} \quad & -150x_1 - 230x_2 - 260x_3 - 238y_1 - 210y_2 \\ & \quad + 170z_1 + 150z_2 + 36z_3 + 10z_4 \\ \text{subject to:} \quad & x_1 + x_2 + x_3 \leq 500 \\ & 2.5x_1 + y_1 - z_1 \geq 200, \qquad 3x_2 + y_2 - z_2 \geq 240 \\ & z_3 + z_4 \leq 20x_3, \qquad z_3 \leq 6000, \qquad x, y, z \geq 0 \end{aligned} \]

About two minutes. Profit is sales minus purchases minus planting. The feed constraints say what you grow plus what you buy, minus what you sell, must cover the feed. With known yields, this is an ordinary LP.

If We Knew the Year

Code 
# Two-stage farm model: one planting plan x, a copy of the purchases y and
# sales z for each scenario. With one scenario it is the ordinary LP.
# Passing `plan` fixes the planting and evaluates it.
function farm_model(factors, probs; plan=nothing)
    n = length(factors)
    model = Model(HiGHS.Optimizer)
    set_silent(model)
    @variable(model, x[1:3] >= 0)             # acres planted
    @variable(model, y[1:2, 1:n] >= 0)        # T bought, per scenario
    @variable(model, z[1:4, 1:n] >= 0)        # T sold, per scenario
    if plan !== nothing
        @constraint(model, x .== plan)
    end
    @constraint(model, sum(x) <= land)
    for s in 1:n
        crop_yield = avg_yield .* factors[s]
        @constraint(model, crop_yield[1] * x[1] + y[1, s] - z[1, s] >= feed_need[1])
        @constraint(model, crop_yield[2] * x[2] + y[2, s] - z[2, s] >= feed_need[2])
        @constraint(model, z[3, s] + z[4, s] <= crop_yield[3] * x[3])
        @constraint(model, z[3, s] <= beet_quota)
    end
    @objective(model, Max, -sum(plant_cost .* x) + sum(probs[s] * (
        sell_price[1] * z[1, s] + sell_price[2] * z[2, s] + beet_price * z[3, s] +
        beet_excess_price * z[4, s] - buy_price[1] * y[1, s] - buy_price[2] * y[2, s])
        for s in 1:n))
    optimize!(model)
    return value.(x), objective_value(model)
end

# The best plan for each year type, if that year were known in advance
known_plan = zeros(3, 3)
known_profit = zeros(3)
for s in 1:3
    known_plan[s, :], known_profit[s] = farm_model([yield_factor[s]], [1])
end
average_plan = known_plan[2, :]

# The two-stage plan: one planting for all three year types
stochastic_plan, stochastic_profit = farm_model(yield_factor, prob)

# Each plan's profit in each year type, with the best purchases and sales
average_plan_by_year = zeros(3)
stochastic_plan_by_year = zeros(3)
for s in 1:3
    average_plan_by_year[s] = farm_model([yield_factor[s]], [1]; plan=average_plan)[2]
    stochastic_plan_by_year[s] = farm_model([yield_factor[s]], [1]; plan=stochastic_plan)[2]
end
eev = sum(prob .* average_plan_by_year)       # average plan, judged under uncertainty
wait_and_see = sum(prob .* known_profit)      # perfect information
vss = stochastic_profit - eev
evpi = wait_and_see - stochastic_profit
Known year Wheat (acres) Corn (acres) Beets (acres) Profit
Average 120 80 300 $118,600
Good 183.3 66.7 250 $167,667
Bad 100 25 375 $59,950

The best plan depends on the year, and planting happens before the year is known.

About three minutes. The folded cell is the whole lecture’s computation: one function that solves the farm problem for any set of scenarios, and can also evaluate a fixed plan. With one scenario it is the ordinary LP. Read the table: in a good year plant less beet land (the quota fills sooner) and more wheat; in a bad year plant more beets to reach the quota and buy corn. The average-year plan earns $118,600, but only if the year is average.

What Changes About the Variables?

What should change about our decision variables?

Variable Copies
\(x_i\), acres planted one (decided before the yield)
\(y_{is}\), T bought one per scenario \(s\)
\(z_{is}\), T sold one per scenario \(s\)

About three minutes. Ask the question first. Planting happens once, so it has one copy. Buying and selling happen after the harvest, so there is a separate copy for each year type. The scenario tree is the bookkeeping: one branch per scenario with its probability. With more uncertainties or more stages, the tree branches again at each one.

One Scenario’s Constraints

Write the good-year constraints (yields \(\times\) 1.2).

\[ \begin{aligned} & 3x_1 + y_{1,\text{good}} - z_{1,\text{good}} \geq 200, \qquad 3.6x_2 + y_{2,\text{good}} - z_{2,\text{good}} \geq 240 \\ & z_{3,\text{good}} + z_{4,\text{good}} \leq 24x_3, \qquad z_{3,\text{good}} \leq 6000 \end{aligned} \]

The average and bad years are the same with yields \(\times\) 1 and \(\times\) 0.8. There is one land constraint, \(x_1 + x_2 + x_3 \leq 500\), shared by all three.

Board item, about four minutes. Give students a minute to write the good-year block from the one-year formulation: every yield is multiplied by 1.2 (2.5 becomes 3, 3 becomes 3.6, 20 becomes 24), and the purchase and sale variables get a good-year subscript. Then point out that the planting variables appear in every scenario’s block unchanged: that is what ties the scenarios together. The full set of constraints is in the appendix.

The Two-Stage Objective

Maximize expected profit: planting cost once, plus each scenario’s sales minus purchases, weighted by its probability.

\[\max_{x, y, z} \quad -\sum_i c_i x_i + \sum_s p_s \left(\text{sales}_s - \text{purchases}_s\right)\]

Other choices are possible: a quantile to hedge against bad years, or the variance of profit to smooth year-to-year swings.

About two minutes. The expected value is one summary of performance across scenarios; it is not the only defensible one. A farmer who cannot survive a bad year might instead maximize the bad-year profit or a low quantile. That choice is a value judgment about risk, and it changes the plan.

The Stochastic Plan

Plan Wheat (acres) Corn (acres) Beets (acres)
Average-year plan 120 80 300
Two-stage plan 170 80 250

Expected profit of the two-stage plan: $108,390.

  • Good year: no beet land wasted above the quota.
  • Bad year: extra wheat profit helps pay for the corn it has to buy.

About three minutes. The two-stage plan moves land from beets to wheat. In a good year the average-year plan would grow more beets than the quota allows, which earns only $10 a tonne; the two-stage plan avoids that. In a bad year both plans fall short on corn, and the extra wheat helps cover the purchase. The plan hedges.

Comparing Plans

Can We Compare These Numbers?

  • Average-year plan: $118,600 profit
  • Two-stage plan: $108,390 expected profit

Is the average-year plan better?

No. $118,600 is what that plan earns if the year is average. To compare fairly, judge both plans across the same three year types.

About two minutes. This is the question that names the issue. The two numbers answer different questions: one is a single-scenario profit on paper, the other is an expected value under uncertainty. Ask before revealing.

Each Plan, Year by Year

Year Average-year plan Two-stage plan
Good $148,000 $167,000
Average $118,600 $109,350
Bad $55,120 $48,820
Expected $107,240 $108,390

Value of the stochastic solution (VSS): $108,390 − $107,240 = $1,150 per year.

Board item for the VSS subtraction, about five minutes. Each plan is evaluated in each year with the best purchases and sales for that year. The average-year plan does well in average and good years but badly in a bad year. Its expected profit under uncertainty is $107,240, less than the two-stage plan’s $108,390. The difference is the value of the stochastic solution: what building the uncertainty into the model is worth. Note the two-stage plan is worse than the average-year plan in the average year itself; it trades some average-year profit for protection in bad years.

What Is a Perfect Forecast Worth?

With perfect foresight the farmer plants the best plan for each year: expected profit $115,406.

Expected value of perfect information (EVPI): $115,406 − $108,390 = $7,016 per year.

Here modelling the uncertainty is worth $1,150 a year, but a perfect forecast would be worth about 6 times as much. The EVPI is the most the farmer should pay for better forecasts.

About four minutes. With perfect information the farmer would know the year before planting and use the best plan for it: the expected profit is the average of the three known-year profits. The gap between that and the two-stage plan is the EVPI. Here it is much larger than the VSS: hedging buys a little, but information would buy a lot more. That is not always the case; it depends on the problem.

Key Takeaways

Key Takeaways

  • The best plan for the average year is not the best plan across years.
  • Two stages: one here-and-now decision, one recourse decision per scenario, weighted by probability.
  • Compare plans under uncertainty: VSS is what modelling uncertainty is worth; EVPI, what a perfect forecast is worth.
  • Scenario trees grow multiplicatively: 3 outcomes a year for 10 years is 59,049 leaves.

About two minutes. The last takeaway sets up Wednesday: with decisions every year and uncertainty every year, the tree explodes, and dynamic programming avoids writing it out.

Appendix

The Full Two-Stage Constraints

\[ \begin{alignedat}{2} &x_1 + x_2 + x_3 \leq 500 \\[0.5ex] &\color{blue}3x_1 + y_{11} - z_{11} \geq 200, && \qquad \color{blue}3.6x_2 + y_{21} - z_{21} \geq 240 \\[0.5ex] &\color{blue}z_{31} + z_{41} \leq 24x_3, && \qquad \color{blue}z_{31} \leq 6000 \\[0.5ex] &\color{purple}2.5x_1 + y_{12} - z_{12} \geq 200, && \qquad \color{purple}3x_2 + y_{22} - z_{22} \geq 240 \\[0.5ex] &\color{purple}z_{32} + z_{42} \leq 20x_3, && \qquad \color{purple}z_{32} \leq 6000 \\[0.5ex] &\color{red}2x_1 + y_{13} - z_{13} \geq 200, && \qquad \color{red}2.4x_2 + y_{23} - z_{23} \geq 240 \\[0.5ex] &\color{red}z_{33} + z_{43} \leq 16x_3, && \qquad \color{red}z_{33} \leq 6000 \\[0.5ex] &x_i, y_{is}, z_{is} \geq 0 \end{alignedat} \]

Scenarios: good (blue), average (purple), bad (red).

General Two-Stage Notation

\[\max_x \; \underbrace{f(x)}_{\text{first stage}} + \mathbb{E}_\xi\left[\underbrace{Q(x; \xi)}_{\substack{\text{best recourse after} \\ \text{seeing } \xi}}\right]\]

With discrete scenarios \(\xi_s\) and probabilities \(p_s\), the expectation is \(\sum_s p_s\, Q(x; \xi_s)\), which is what the farmer model maximizes.
